rationales: Laboratory manufacture is small-scale, not industrial-scale production.
Microscale manufacture is not the commercial production meant by industrial chemistry.
Industrial chemistry concerns manufacturing compounds on a commercial scale.
Domestic-scale production is not the defining scale of industrial chemistry.
Protons are charged and are less penetrating than neutrons in this comparison.
Electrons can penetrate more than alpha particles, but are not the most penetrating option here.
Neutrons have no electric charge, allowing them to penetrate matter more readily than the listed charged particles.
Alpha particles are strongly ionizing and have low penetrating power.
Lattice energy relates to the formation of an ionic crystal lattice, not electron addition to an atom.
Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an atom.
Electronegativity measures an atom’s tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond.
Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom.
Mendeleev’s table was primarily organized by atomic mass, not by this postulate.
The long-form periodic table is arranged according to increasing atomic number.
Atomic mass was the basis of Mendeleev’s arrangement, not the modern long-form table.
Mass number is not the basis used to arrange the long-form periodic table.
Donation of electrons alone describes electron transfer, not covalent bonding.
Acceptance of electrons alone describes electron transfer, not covalent bonding.
A covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pairs.
Repulsion of electrons does not form a covalent bond.
NH₃ has a complete octet around its nitrogen atom.
BF₃ is electron deficient because boron has only six electrons around it in the molecule.
N₂ has a triple bond and both nitrogen atoms achieve complete octets.
O₂ has a covalent structure in which both oxygen atoms achieve complete octets.
O₂ and Cl₂ contain bonds between identical atoms, so their bonds are nonpolar.
H₂O has polar bonds, but N₂ has a nonpolar bond between identical nitrogen atoms.
H₂O has polar bonds, whereas C₂H₂ is treated as having essentially nonpolar covalent bonds at this level.
Both H₂O and HCl contain polar covalent bonds.
The Tyndall effect is not caused by blockage of the light beam.
A beam that is not scattered does not produce the Tyndall effect.
The Tyndall effect occurs when colloidal particles scatter a beam of light.
The effect is not simply light passing through without interaction.
Hydrogen is oxidized and oxygen is reduced during water formation, so the reaction is redox.
The reaction does not involve an acid reacting with a base.
Water formation from hydrogen and oxygen is not an acid–base neutralization.
The reaction combines elements to form a compound rather than decomposing one.
Sodium does not react directly with nitrogen under ordinary conditions to form a nitride.
Sodium can react with hydrogen to form sodium hydride under suitable conditions.
Sodium is not generally described as being unable to react directly with carbon under suitable conditions.
Sodium can react with phosphorus to form a phosphide.
Butter is a familiar example of liquid dispersed in a solid-like medium.
Air is a mixture of gases, not a liquid-in-solid solution.
Brass is a solid solution of metals, not a liquid-in-solid solution.
Alcohol in water is a liquid dissolved in a liquid.
Liquids are generally much more than 100 times as dense as gases.
Liquids are approximately 1000 times denser than gases in the usual textbook comparison.
The usual comparison is about 1000 times, not 10000 times.
The usual comparison is about 1000 times, not 100000 times.
Starch dispersed in water can form a colloid, so this may also be a valid answer.
Paint is a colloid, but starch dispersions can also be colloids, making the question ambiguous.
Milk of magnesia is generally treated as a suspension rather than the intended colloid example.
Chalk in water is a suspension because its particles settle on standing.
Tin can corrode, but the familiar example of rusting is not tin.
Aluminium forms an oxide layer rather than the common rust referred to here.
Rusting of iron is the most common textbook example of corrosion.
Zinc can corrode, but rusting of iron is the standard example.
Sodium is soft and not as malleable as gold.
Iron is malleable but less so than gold.
Gold is the most malleable metal among these options.
Potassium is soft and not as malleable as gold.
